passages.title: The family list changes its wording at Jesus' birth
passages.summary: Matthew opens with the family line of Jesus Christ, son of David and Abraham. It runs in three sets of fourteen generations. Four women appear in it: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Uriah’s wife. Mary is pledged to Joseph and is found with child by the Holy Spirit. Joseph plans to end the engagement quietly. An angel tells him in a dream to take Mary as his wife. The child will be named Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins. Joseph does as he is told.
passages.uncertainty: The points mark places this chapter names, as settings or in speech. The exact houses, roads, and tombs are not known.

lds.text: The 2023 lesson studies Joseph’s response and faith in Jesus, the Son of God. Why does the family list change its wording when it reaches Joseph and Mary?

contextNote.title: The family list changes its wording at Jesus' birth
contextNote.text: The list says about forty times that a man “became the father of” a son. Verse 16 breaks that pattern. Joseph is called the husband of Mary. Jesus is then said to be born “from whom,” meaning from her. Matthew does not say Joseph fathered him. Verses 18–25 explain the change. The four women named earlier also entered the line in unexpected ways.

passages.title: The child's escape exposes the ruler's violence
passages.summary: Wise men from the east come to Jerusalem seeking the newborn king of the Jews. King Herod is troubled and learns the Christ should be born in Bethlehem. The star leads the wise men to the child, and they worship him with gifts. A dream warns them not to return to Herod. An angel tells Joseph to flee to Egypt with the child and his mother. Herod kills the young boys of Bethlehem. After Herod dies, Joseph brings the family back. They settle in Nazareth in Galilee.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Matthew names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Why does Matthew keep the other children’s deaths beside the child’s escape?

contextNote.title: The child's escape exposes the ruler's violence
contextNote.text: Foreigners travel far to honor the child. The king of the land plans to kill him. Verse 13 saves the child by a warning and a night journey. Verse 16 shows that other children were not spared. Matthew does not explain that or soften it. He quotes Rachel weeping for her children (verse 18). The escape is told beside the grief of Bethlehem.

passages.title: John demands changed conduct before inherited status
passages.summary: John the Baptist preaches in the desert of Judea. He tells people to repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is near. He wears camel’s hair and eats locusts and wild honey. Crowds come and are baptized in the Jordan, confessing their sins. He warns the Pharisees and Sadducees to bear fruit that fits repentance. They must not rely on having Abraham as their father. Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized. The Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice calls him God’s beloved Son.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Matthew names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Why does John demand visible fruit rather than claims about ancestry?

contextNote.title: John demands changed conduct before inherited status
contextNote.text: John addresses religious leaders in verses 7–10. Verse 8 demands fruit, meaning conduct that shows a changed life. Verse 9 names the claim they might use: descent from Abraham. John says God can raise children for Abraham from stones. Ancestry gives no protection. The ax is already at the root of the trees (verse 10). Being baptized is not enough without the change it stands for.

passages.title: Scripture becomes a dispute over how the Son should act
passages.summary: The Spirit leads Jesus into the desert, where he fasts forty days. The devil tells him to turn stones into bread. He tells him to throw himself from the temple and trust the angels. He offers all the world’s kingdoms in return for worship. Jesus answers each time from Deuteronomy. He then begins to preach in Galilee. He calls four fishermen, who leave their nets and follow him. He heals the sick, and great crowds gather.

lds.text: How does the second temptation show that quoting Scripture alone cannot settle the dispute?

contextNote.title: Scripture becomes a dispute over how the Son should act
contextNote.text: In the second test the devil quotes Psalm 91:11–12. Both speakers are now using Scripture. Verse 7 answers with “Again, it is written.” Jesus sets one text beside another. Quoting a verse does not settle how to act. The devil uses a promise as a reason to force God’s hand. Jesus reads it within the command not to test God (Deuteronomy 6:16).

passages.title: Repaired relationships belong before the offering
passages.summary: Jesus goes up a mountain and teaches his disciples. He calls the poor in spirit, the mourners, and the merciful blessed. His followers are salt and light. He has come to fulfill the law, not to destroy it. Anger and insult are judged along with murder. He speaks about lust, divorce, oaths, and revenge. He tells them to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. They are to be complete, as their Father is.

lds.text: The selected 2023 lesson studies blessed lives and reads completeness through Christ. Why must repairing the relationship come before completing the offering?

contextNote.title: Repaired relationships belong before the offering
contextNote.text: Verses 21–22 trace murder back to anger and insult. Verses 23–24 then give a case. A person stands at the altar with an offering. He remembers that a brother has something against him. The verse does not ask who was at fault. He must leave the gift and go to be reconciled first. Worship waits for the repaired relationship.

passages.title: Hidden worship and divided service test the same heart
passages.summary: Jesus warns against doing good in order to be seen. Giving, prayer, and fasting should be done in secret before the Father. He gives his disciples a prayer to use. They must forgive others as they ask to be forgiven. They should store treasure in heaven and not on earth. No one can serve two masters. They should not be anxious about food or clothing. They should seek God’s Kingdom first.

lds.text: How do public admiration and stored treasure place competing claims on the heart?

contextNote.title: Hidden worship and divided service test the same heart
contextNote.text: The chapter names two rivals for the heart. Verses 1–18 concern the wish to be admired. Verses 19–24 concern stored wealth. Verse 24 says a person cannot serve God and Mammon. Mammon means wealth treated as a master. Each rival offers a reward now: praise or security. Verses 25–34 follow with the worry that comes from serving wealth.

passages.title: Hearing becomes secure only through action
passages.summary: Jesus warns against judging others while ignoring one’s own faults. He tells his hearers to ask, seek, and knock. They should treat others as they want to be treated. The gate to life is narrow. False prophets are known by their fruit. Not everyone who calls him Lord will enter the Kingdom. The one who hears and acts is like a house built on rock. The crowds are amazed at his authority.

lds.text: What separates the two builders when both hear the same teaching?

contextNote.title: Hearing becomes secure only through action
contextNote.text: The sermon ends with two builders. Both hear the same words (verses 24 and 26). Both build a house, and the same storm strikes both. Only one thing separates them. The first “does” what he heard, and the second does not. Hearing, agreeing, and admiring are not the foundation. Verses 21–23 have just warned that saying “Lord” is not enough.

passages.title: Authority brings healing but does not guarantee welcome
passages.summary: Jesus comes down from the mountain and heals a man with a skin disease. A Roman officer asks him to heal a paralyzed servant. The officer says Jesus need only speak the word. Jesus marvels at his faith and heals the servant. He heals Peter’s mother-in-law and many others. He warns would-be followers of the cost. He calms a storm on the lake. Across the water he frees two men from demons, and the town sends him away.

lds.text: Why does the officer describe his own authority when asking Jesus for help?

contextNote.title: Authority brings healing but does not guarantee welcome
contextNote.text: The officer explains his request by describing his own work. He lives under orders, and he gives them (verse 9). A word from him is enough to move soldiers. He reasons that Jesus has that kind of authority over sickness. Jesus need not come to the house. Verse 10 says Jesus found no such faith in Israel. The chapter ends with a town that asks him to go (verse 34).

passages.title: Mercy challenges the boundaries around a shared meal
passages.summary: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, and scribes accuse him of blasphemy. He calls Matthew, a tax collector, who follows him. He eats with tax collectors and sinners, and Pharisees object. He says the sick are the ones who need a doctor. He raises a ruler’s daughter and heals a woman who touches his cloak. He gives sight to two blind men and speech to a mute man. He has compassion on the crowds, who are like sheep without a shepherd. He tells his disciples to pray for workers.

lds.text: How does the physician comparison answer criticism of the shared meal?

contextNote.title: Mercy challenges the boundaries around a shared meal
contextNote.text: The Pharisees object to the company at the table (verse 11). Verse 12 answers with a doctor, who goes where the sick are. Verse 13 then sends the critics back to Scripture. They should learn Hosea 6:6: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.” Their care for purity has left out mercy. Jesus says he came to call sinners. The meal is the cure at work.

passages.title: The sent disciples depend on those who receive them
passages.summary: Jesus calls twelve disciples and gives them authority to heal. He sends them to the lost sheep of Israel. They must give freely, as they have freely received. They carry no money or extra clothes and stay with those who welcome them. They will be arrested and hated for his name. They should not fear those who can kill only the body. Family members will turn against each other. Whoever receives them receives Jesus.

lds.text: What makes receiving a traveling disciple part of receiving Jesus?

contextNote.title: The sent disciples depend on those who receive them
contextNote.text: Verse 8 tells the twelve to heal and to charge nothing. They received freely, so they give freely. Verses 9–10 then take away their supplies. They carry no money, bag, or spare coat. They must depend on the households that take them in. The plan ties the messengers to their hosts. Verses 40–42 say that welcoming them counts as welcoming Jesus.

passages.title: John's question meets evidence of healing rather than a title alone
passages.summary: John the Baptist is in prison and hears what Jesus is doing. He sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one to come. Jesus tells them to report what they see and hear. He praises John as more than a prophet. He says this generation is like children who are never satisfied. He rebukes towns that saw his works and did not repent. He thanks the Father for showing these things to little children. He invites the weary to come and find rest.

lds.text: Why does Jesus answer John with acts of healing and good news?

contextNote.title: John's question meets evidence of healing rather than a title alone
contextNote.text: John asks a direct question in verse 3. Jesus does not answer with a title. Verse 5 lists what is happening. The blind see, the lame walk, and the poor hear good news. The list echoes Isaiah 35:5–6 and 61:1. John is left to draw the conclusion from the evidence. Verse 6 adds a blessing for anyone who does not stumble over him.

passages.title: Mercy answers accusations while the conflict becomes dangerous
passages.summary: The disciples pick grain on the Sabbath because they are hungry. Pharisees say this is unlawful. Jesus recalls that David ate holy bread when he was hungry. He heals a man’s withered hand in the synagogue. The Pharisees plan to destroy him. He frees a blind and mute man, and they credit the ruler of demons. He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand. He says whoever does his Father’s will is his family.

lds.text: How does the hungry disciples’ situation shape the Sabbath argument?

contextNote.title: Mercy answers accusations while the conflict becomes dangerous
contextNote.text: Verse 1 gives the reason for the disciples’ act: they were hungry. Jesus answers from Scripture with David’s hunger (verses 3–4). Verse 7 quotes Hosea 6:6 again, as in 9:13. Mercy matters more than the rule as his critics apply it. He calls the disciples “guiltless.” The dispute then grows dangerous. Verse 14 says the Pharisees began to plan his death.

passages.title: The field stories examine hearing, growth, and premature judgment
passages.summary: Jesus teaches the crowds from a boat with stories. A farmer sows seed on four kinds of soil. An enemy sows weeds among a man’s wheat. The Kingdom is like a mustard seed and like yeast in flour. It is like hidden treasure, a fine pearl, and a net full of fish. He explains the stories to his disciples in private. He goes to his home town, and the people take offense. He does few mighty works there.

lds.text: Why does the owner stop servants from removing the weeds immediately?

contextNote.title: The field stories examine hearing, growth, and premature judgment
contextNote.text: In the second story servants find weeds among the wheat. They offer to pull them out (verse 28). Verse 29 gives the owner’s reason for refusing. Pulling the weeds now would uproot wheat as well. The two look alike while they grow. Sorting belongs to the harvest and to the reapers (verse 30). The story warns against judging who belongs before the time.

passages.title: Two meals reveal sharply different uses of power
passages.summary: Herod the ruler hears about Jesus and thinks he is John risen from the dead. Herod had jailed John for condemning his marriage. At his birthday feast a girl’s dance pleases him, and he promises her anything. She asks for John’s head, and he gives the order. Jesus withdraws, and crowds follow him. He feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. He walks on the sea to his disciples at night. Peter steps out, sinks, and is caught by Jesus.

lds.text: What does each meal show about the person who directs it?

contextNote.title: Two meals reveal sharply different uses of power
contextNote.text: The chapter sets two meals side by side. Herod’s feast is for the powerful. Verse 9 says he was grieved and still gave the order. His oath and his guests mattered more to him than a life. The meal ends with a head on a platter. Jesus’s meal is in a deserted place for hungry crowds (verses 15–21). It ends with everyone fed and food left over.

passages.title: The woman's reply presses against the stated boundary
passages.summary: Pharisees ask why the disciples do not wash their hands before eating. Jesus says they set aside God’s command for their tradition. What comes out of the mouth defiles a person, not what goes in. He travels to the region of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman begs him to heal her daughter. He says he was sent to Israel, and she keeps asking. He praises her faith and heals the girl. Back in Galilee he heals many and feeds four thousand.

lds.text: How does the woman’s reply use the same image that excludes her?

contextNote.title: The woman's reply presses against the stated boundary
contextNote.text: Jesus says it is not right to give the children’s bread to dogs (verse 26). She does not reject the picture. Verse 27 works inside it. Even the dogs eat what falls from the table. She asks only for crumbs. Verse 28 calls her faith great, and her daughter is healed. A foreign woman’s answer presses past a stated limit.

passages.title: Peter recognizes Jesus but rejects the suffering he announces
passages.summary: Pharisees and Sadducees ask Jesus for a sign from heaven. He warns his disciples about their teaching. He asks the disciples who they say he is. Peter answers that he is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus blesses him and speaks of building his assembly. Then he says he must suffer, be killed, and rise. Peter rebukes him, and Jesus calls him a stumbling block. Anyone who follows him must take up a cross.

lds.text: Doctrine and Covenants 128:10 quotes verses 18–19 about binding on earth. Why can Peter confess Jesus’ identity and still oppose his announced path?

contextNote.title: Peter recognizes Jesus but rejects the suffering he announces
contextNote.text: Peter gives the right answer in verse 16 and is blessed for it. In verse 22 he tells Jesus that suffering must never happen. Verse 23 uses the harshest words in the chapter for the same man. Peter is thinking in human terms. He knows who Jesus is and rejects the path Jesus names. Knowing the title is not the same as accepting what it means. Verses 24–25 apply that path to every follower.

passages.title: The mountain's glory does not remove the coming suffering
passages.summary: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. His face shines like the sun, and Moses and Elijah appear with him. Peter offers to build three shelters. A bright cloud covers them, and a voice calls Jesus the beloved Son. The disciples fall down afraid, and Jesus touches them. He tells them to say nothing until he has risen. Below, he heals a boy the disciples could not heal. He again says he will be killed and raised.
passages.uncertainty: The points mark places this chapter names, as settings or in speech. The exact houses, roads, and tombs are not known.

lds.text: How does the suffering discussed afterward change the meaning of the mountain scene?

contextNote.title: The mountain's glory does not remove the coming suffering
contextNote.text: The voice in verse 5 repeats the words spoken at Jesus’s baptism (3:17). It adds a command: “Listen to him.” What he has just said is that he must suffer (16:21). On the way down he speaks of it again (verses 9 and 12). Verses 22–23 repeat it once more, and the disciples grieve. The glory on the mountain does not cancel that path. It tells them to trust the one who walks it.

passages.title: Care for the small and mercy for debtors answer the rank question
passages.summary: The disciples ask who is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven. Jesus sets a child among them and tells them to become like children. He warns against causing little ones to stumble. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one that strayed. He teaches how to deal with a brother who sins. Peter asks how often he must forgive. Jesus tells of a servant forgiven a huge debt. That servant jails a man who owes him little and is punished.

lds.text: The selected 2023 lesson connects receiving forgiveness with forgiving others. Why does the king ask the forgiven debtor about mercy toward his fellow servant?

contextNote.title: Care for the small and mercy for debtors answer the rank question
contextNote.text: The first servant owed ten thousand talents, a sum no one could repay (verse 24). The second owed a hundred denarii, a few months’ wages (verse 28). The king forgave the larger debt entirely. Verse 33 asks the question the story turns on. Should the forgiven man not have shown the same mercy? Forgiveness received was meant to change how he treated others. The chapter began with a question about rank and ends here.

passages.title: Possessions expose the cost hidden inside the young man's question
passages.summary: Pharisees test Jesus with a question about divorce. He points them to the beginning, when God joined man and woman. People bring children, and he blesses them. A rich young man asks what good thing he must do to have eternal life. He says he has kept the commandments. Jesus tells him to sell what he has and give to the poor. The young man goes away sad. Jesus says the last will be first.

lds.text: What does the young man’s sorrow reveal about the demand Jesus makes?

contextNote.title: Possessions expose the cost hidden inside the young man's question
contextNote.text: The young man asks what he still lacks (verse 20). Verse 21 answers with one demand and one invitation. He should sell his goods, give to the poor, and follow. Verse 22 says he left sad, since he owned much. His sadness shows where the cost lay. He had kept the rules and could not let go of his wealth. Verse 26 says such a change is possible only with God.

passages.title: Equal pay and serving challenge the pursuit of rank
passages.summary: Jesus tells of a landowner who hires workers at dawn for a day’s wage. He hires more at later hours, even an hour before sunset. At evening each receives the same wage. Those hired first complain. Jesus again foretells his death and resurrection. The mother of James and John asks for the best seats for her sons. Jesus says the great must be servants. He gives sight to two blind men near Jericho.

lds.text: Why do the earlier workers resent receiving exactly the wage they agreed upon?

contextNote.title: Equal pay and serving challenge the pursuit of rank
contextNote.text: The first workers received exactly what they agreed to (verse 13). No one cheated them. Verse 12 states their real complaint. The owner made the latecomers “equal to us.” They resent another’s gain, not their own loss. The owner asks whether his generosity makes them envious (verse 15). The request for the best seats shows the same concern for rank (verses 20–21).

passages.title: The vineyard accusation names its immediate hearers
passages.summary: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, and crowds shout “Hosanna.” He drives the traders out of the temple and heals there. The chief priests ask by what authority he acts. He answers with a question about John’s baptism. He tells of two sons, only one of whom obeys. He tells of tenants who kill the owner’s servants and then his son. He says the Kingdom will be given to others. The leaders want to arrest him and fear the crowds.

lds.text: Whom does the chapter identify as the immediate hearers of the vineyard accusation?

contextNote.title: The vineyard accusation names its immediate hearers
contextNote.text: The vineyard story uses a picture from Isaiah 5:1–7. In it the tenants refuse to give the owner his fruit. Verse 45 says who understood themselves to be the target. The chief priests and the Pharisees saw that he meant them. The charge is aimed at those leaders in that place. Verse 46 shows the crowds on the other side, holding Jesus to be a prophet. The story should not be read as a charge against a whole people.

passages.title: Tests about taxes and resurrection lead to love as the law's center
passages.summary: Jesus tells of a king whose invited guests refuse his son’s wedding feast. The Pharisees ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. He says to give Caesar what is Caesar’s and God what is God’s. The Sadducees ask about marriage in the resurrection. He says God is the God of the living. A lawyer asks which commandment is greatest. Jesus names love for God and love for neighbor. He then asks how the Christ can be David’s son and David’s Lord.

lds.text: How does the answer about love hold the law’s different demands together?

contextNote.title: Tests about taxes and resurrection lead to love as the law's center
contextNote.text: The lawyer asks for one great commandment (verse 36). Jesus gives two and joins them. The first is from Deuteronomy 6:5, and the second from Leviticus 19:18. Verse 40 says all the law and the prophets “depend” on these. The word pictures something hanging from a peg. Every other command hangs from love of God and neighbor. They are the measure for reading the rest.

passages.title: The accusation examines burdens, display, and neglected justice
passages.summary: Jesus speaks to the crowds and his disciples about the scribes and Pharisees. They teach the law and do not practice it. They load others with heavy burdens and love titles and honor. He pronounces a series of woes on them. They shut the Kingdom against people. They tithe small herbs and neglect justice, mercy, and faith. They are like whitewashed tombs. He grieves over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets.

lds.text: Why does the spice tithe example place small obedience beside neglected justice?

contextNote.title: The accusation examines burdens, display, and neglected justice
contextNote.text: Verse 23 gives an example of careful obedience. These teachers tithe even garden herbs. Jesus does not tell them to stop. He says they “ought to have done” the weightier things as well. Those are justice, mercy, and faith. Small duties have crowded out large ones. Verse 37 shows that the speech ends in grief over the city.

passages.title: Readiness means faithful care during an uncertain wait
passages.summary: Jesus says the temple’s stones will all be thrown down. On the Mount of Olives his disciples ask when and what the sign will be. He warns of false christs, wars, famines, and persecution. They must flee when they see the desolating sacrilege. The Son of Man will come like lightning. No one knows the day or hour, not even the angels. As in Noah’s days, people will be caught unaware. So they must watch and be ready.

lds.text: Joseph Smith—Matthew gives Joseph Smith’s translation of this chapter. What distinguishes the faithful servant’s conduct during the delay?

contextNote.title: Readiness means faithful care during an uncertain wait
contextNote.text: The disciples ask for a date and a sign (verse 3). Verse 36 says the day is unknown. Verses 45–51 then describe what readiness looks like. A servant is set over the household to give them food on time. The faithful one is found doing that when his master returns. The bad servant beats the others and gets drunk. Being ready means caring for people during the wait.

passages.title: The waiting stories end with care for people in need
passages.summary: Jesus tells of ten young women waiting with lamps for a bridegroom. Five run out of oil and are shut out. He tells of a man who entrusts money to three servants. Two put it to work, and one buries it. Then he describes the Son of Man on his throne. He separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Some fed the hungry, welcomed strangers, and visited prisoners. The King says they did it to him.

lds.text: Why are both groups surprised by the king’s explanation of their treatment of him?

contextNote.title: The waiting stories end with care for people in need
contextNote.text: Both groups in the last scene are surprised. The first asks when they saw the King hungry or in prison (verses 37–39). The second asks the same question (verse 44). Neither knew who was in front of them. Verse 40 gives the King’s explanation. What was done for the least of his brothers was done for him. The chapter’s stories of waiting end with care for people in need.

passages.title: Jesus' arrest reveals failed promises and rejected force
passages.summary: The chief priests plot to kill Jesus, and a woman anoints him with costly oil. Judas agrees to hand him over for thirty pieces of silver. Jesus eats the Passover with the twelve and gives them bread and the cup. Peter promises never to deny him. In Gethsemane Jesus prays while the disciples sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd, and Jesus is arrested. The council condemns him for blasphemy. Peter denies knowing him three times and weeps.

lds.text: How does Jesus’ rejection of the sword differ from the arresting crowd’s use of force?

contextNote.title: Jesus' arrest reveals failed promises and rejected force
contextNote.text: A crowd comes with swords and clubs (verse 47). One of Jesus’s companions draws a sword and strikes (verse 51). Verse 52 tells him to put it away. Those who take the sword will die by it. Jesus says he could call on legions of angels (verse 53). He refuses force from his own side as well. Verse 56 then says all the disciples left him and fled.

passages.title: The governor's handwashing does not stop his order
passages.summary: Jesus is handed to Pilate, the governor. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself. Pilate questions Jesus and offers to release a prisoner. The crowd asks for Barabbas. Pilate washes his hands and says he is innocent of this blood. Soldiers mock Jesus with a robe, a crown of thorns, and a reed. He is crucified between two robbers and dies. Joseph of Arimathea buries him, and the tomb is sealed and guarded.

lds.text: How do Pilate’s actions differ from his public claim of innocence?

contextNote.title: The governor's handwashing does not stop his order
contextNote.text: Pilate’s wife warns him that Jesus is righteous (verse 19). Pilate himself sees that envy lies behind the charge (verse 18). In verse 24 he washes his hands in front of the crowd. Verse 26 then reports what he does. He has Jesus flogged and hands him over to be crucified. The order is his. A public gesture does not undo the act that follows it.

passages.title: The final promise sends uncertain disciples beyond the earlier boundary
passages.summary: At dawn after the Sabbath two women come to the tomb. An angel rolls back the stone and tells them Jesus has risen. They run to tell the disciples and meet Jesus on the way. The guards are paid to say the body was stolen. The eleven go to a mountain in Galilee. They worship him, though some doubt. He says all authority has been given to him. He sends them to make disciples of all nations and promises to be with them.

lds.text: The selected 2023 lesson teaches resurrection through the Gospel accounts. How does the closing promise connect with the opening name Immanuel?

contextNote.title: The final promise sends uncertain disciples beyond the earlier boundary
contextNote.text: Verse 17 says the eleven worshiped and that some doubted. Jesus sends them anyway. In 10:5–6 he sent them only to Israel. Verse 19 now sends them to all nations. Verse 20 closes the book with a promise: “I am with you always.” The book opened with the name Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23). The promise that began it also ends it.

events.title: The family list changes its wording at Jesus' birth
events.summary: Matthew opens with the family line of Jesus Christ, son of David and Abraham. It runs in three sets of fourteen generations. Four women appear in it: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Uriah’s wife. Mary is pledged to Joseph and is found with child by the Holy Spirit. Joseph plans to end the engagement quietly. An angel tells him in a dream to take Mary as his wife. The child will be named Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins. Joseph does as he is told.
events.detail: The list says about forty times that a man “became the father of” a son. Verse 16 breaks that pattern. Joseph is called the husband of Mary. Jesus is then said to be born “from whom,” meaning from her. Matthew does not say Joseph fathered him. Verses 18–25 explain the change. The four women named earlier also entered the line in unexpected ways.

events.title: The child's escape exposes the ruler's violence
events.summary: Wise men from the east come to Jerusalem seeking the newborn king of the Jews. King Herod is troubled and learns the Christ should be born in Bethlehem. The star leads the wise men to the child, and they worship him with gifts. A dream warns them not to return to Herod. An angel tells Joseph to flee to Egypt with the child and his mother. Herod kills the young boys of Bethlehem. After Herod dies, Joseph brings the family back. They settle in Nazareth in Galilee.
events.detail: Foreigners travel far to honor the child. The king of the land plans to kill him. Verse 13 saves the child by a warning and a night journey. Verse 16 shows that other children were not spared. Matthew does not explain that or soften it. He quotes Rachel weeping for her children (verse 18). The escape is told beside the grief of Bethlehem.

events.title: John demands changed conduct before inherited status
events.summary: John the Baptist preaches in the desert of Judea. He tells people to repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is near. He wears camel’s hair and eats locusts and wild honey. Crowds come and are baptized in the Jordan, confessing their sins. He warns the Pharisees and Sadducees to bear fruit that fits repentance. They must not rely on having Abraham as their father. Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized. The Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice calls him God’s beloved Son.
events.detail: John addresses religious leaders in verses 7–10. Verse 8 demands fruit, meaning conduct that shows a changed life. Verse 9 names the claim they might use: descent from Abraham. John says God can raise children for Abraham from stones. Ancestry gives no protection. The ax is already at the root of the trees (verse 10). Being baptized is not enough without the change it stands for.

events.title: Scripture becomes a dispute over how the Son should act
events.summary: The Spirit leads Jesus into the desert, where he fasts forty days. The devil tells him to turn stones into bread. He tells him to throw himself from the temple and trust the angels. He offers all the world’s kingdoms in return for worship. Jesus answers each time from Deuteronomy. He then begins to preach in Galilee. He calls four fishermen, who leave their nets and follow him. He heals the sick, and great crowds gather.
events.detail: In the second test the devil quotes Psalm 91:11–12. Both speakers are now using Scripture. Verse 7 answers with “Again, it is written.” Jesus sets one text beside another. Quoting a verse does not settle how to act. The devil uses a promise as a reason to force God’s hand. Jesus reads it within the command not to test God (Deuteronomy 6:16).

events.title: Repaired relationships belong before the offering
events.summary: Jesus goes up a mountain and teaches his disciples. He calls the poor in spirit, the mourners, and the merciful blessed. His followers are salt and light. He has come to fulfill the law, not to destroy it. Anger and insult are judged along with murder. He speaks about lust, divorce, oaths, and revenge. He tells them to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. They are to be complete, as their Father is.
events.detail: Verses 21–22 trace murder back to anger and insult. Verses 23–24 then give a case. A person stands at the altar with an offering. He remembers that a brother has something against him. The verse does not ask who was at fault. He must leave the gift and go to be reconciled first. Worship waits for the repaired relationship.

events.title: Hidden worship and divided service test the same heart
events.summary: Jesus warns against doing good in order to be seen. Giving, prayer, and fasting should be done in secret before the Father. He gives his disciples a prayer to use. They must forgive others as they ask to be forgiven. They should store treasure in heaven and not on earth. No one can serve two masters. They should not be anxious about food or clothing. They should seek God’s Kingdom first.
events.detail: The chapter names two rivals for the heart. Verses 1–18 concern the wish to be admired. Verses 19–24 concern stored wealth. Verse 24 says a person cannot serve God and Mammon. Mammon means wealth treated as a master. Each rival offers a reward now: praise or security. Verses 25–34 follow with the worry that comes from serving wealth.

events.title: Hearing becomes secure only through action
events.summary: Jesus warns against judging others while ignoring one’s own faults. He tells his hearers to ask, seek, and knock. They should treat others as they want to be treated. The gate to life is narrow. False prophets are known by their fruit. Not everyone who calls him Lord will enter the Kingdom. The one who hears and acts is like a house built on rock. The crowds are amazed at his authority.
events.detail: The sermon ends with two builders. Both hear the same words (verses 24 and 26). Both build a house, and the same storm strikes both. Only one thing separates them. The first “does” what he heard, and the second does not. Hearing, agreeing, and admiring are not the foundation. Verses 21–23 have just warned that saying “Lord” is not enough.

events.title: Authority brings healing but does not guarantee welcome
events.summary: Jesus comes down from the mountain and heals a man with a skin disease. A Roman officer asks him to heal a paralyzed servant. The officer says Jesus need only speak the word. Jesus marvels at his faith and heals the servant. He heals Peter’s mother-in-law and many others. He warns would-be followers of the cost. He calms a storm on the lake. Across the water he frees two men from demons, and the town sends him away.
events.detail: The officer explains his request by describing his own work. He lives under orders, and he gives them (verse 9). A word from him is enough to move soldiers. He reasons that Jesus has that kind of authority over sickness. Jesus need not come to the house. Verse 10 says Jesus found no such faith in Israel. The chapter ends with a town that asks him to go (verse 34).

events.title: Mercy challenges the boundaries around a shared meal
events.summary: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, and scribes accuse him of blasphemy. He calls Matthew, a tax collector, who follows him. He eats with tax collectors and sinners, and Pharisees object. He says the sick are the ones who need a doctor. He raises a ruler’s daughter and heals a woman who touches his cloak. He gives sight to two blind men and speech to a mute man. He has compassion on the crowds, who are like sheep without a shepherd. He tells his disciples to pray for workers.
events.detail: The Pharisees object to the company at the table (verse 11). Verse 12 answers with a doctor, who goes where the sick are. Verse 13 then sends the critics back to Scripture. They should learn Hosea 6:6: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.” Their care for purity has left out mercy. Jesus says he came to call sinners. The meal is the cure at work.

events.title: The sent disciples depend on those who receive them
events.summary: Jesus calls twelve disciples and gives them authority to heal. He sends them to the lost sheep of Israel. They must give freely, as they have freely received. They carry no money or extra clothes and stay with those who welcome them. They will be arrested and hated for his name. They should not fear those who can kill only the body. Family members will turn against each other. Whoever receives them receives Jesus.
events.detail: Verse 8 tells the twelve to heal and to charge nothing. They received freely, so they give freely. Verses 9–10 then take away their supplies. They carry no money, bag, or spare coat. They must depend on the households that take them in. The plan ties the messengers to their hosts. Verses 40–42 say that welcoming them counts as welcoming Jesus.

events.title: John's question meets evidence of healing rather than a title alone
events.summary: John the Baptist is in prison and hears what Jesus is doing. He sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one to come. Jesus tells them to report what they see and hear. He praises John as more than a prophet. He says this generation is like children who are never satisfied. He rebukes towns that saw his works and did not repent. He thanks the Father for showing these things to little children. He invites the weary to come and find rest.
events.detail: John asks a direct question in verse 3. Jesus does not answer with a title. Verse 5 lists what is happening. The blind see, the lame walk, and the poor hear good news. The list echoes Isaiah 35:5–6 and 61:1. John is left to draw the conclusion from the evidence. Verse 6 adds a blessing for anyone who does not stumble over him.

events.title: Mercy answers accusations while the conflict becomes dangerous
events.summary: The disciples pick grain on the Sabbath because they are hungry. Pharisees say this is unlawful. Jesus recalls that David ate holy bread when he was hungry. He heals a man’s withered hand in the synagogue. The Pharisees plan to destroy him. He frees a blind and mute man, and they credit the ruler of demons. He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand. He says whoever does his Father’s will is his family.
events.detail: Verse 1 gives the reason for the disciples’ act: they were hungry. Jesus answers from Scripture with David’s hunger (verses 3–4). Verse 7 quotes Hosea 6:6 again, as in 9:13. Mercy matters more than the rule as his critics apply it. He calls the disciples “guiltless.” The dispute then grows dangerous. Verse 14 says the Pharisees began to plan his death.

events.title: The field stories examine hearing, growth, and premature judgment
events.summary: Jesus teaches the crowds from a boat with stories. A farmer sows seed on four kinds of soil. An enemy sows weeds among a man’s wheat. The Kingdom is like a mustard seed and like yeast in flour. It is like hidden treasure, a fine pearl, and a net full of fish. He explains the stories to his disciples in private. He goes to his home town, and the people take offense. He does few mighty works there.
events.detail: In the second story servants find weeds among the wheat. They offer to pull them out (verse 28). Verse 29 gives the owner’s reason for refusing. Pulling the weeds now would uproot wheat as well. The two look alike while they grow. Sorting belongs to the harvest and to the reapers (verse 30). The story warns against judging who belongs before the time.

events.title: Two meals reveal sharply different uses of power
events.summary: Herod the ruler hears about Jesus and thinks he is John risen from the dead. Herod had jailed John for condemning his marriage. At his birthday feast a girl’s dance pleases him, and he promises her anything. She asks for John’s head, and he gives the order. Jesus withdraws, and crowds follow him. He feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. He walks on the sea to his disciples at night. Peter steps out, sinks, and is caught by Jesus.
events.detail: The chapter sets two meals side by side. Herod’s feast is for the powerful. Verse 9 says he was grieved and still gave the order. His oath and his guests mattered more to him than a life. The meal ends with a head on a platter. Jesus’s meal is in a deserted place for hungry crowds (verses 15–21). It ends with everyone fed and food left over.

events.title: The woman's reply presses against the stated boundary
events.summary: Pharisees ask why the disciples do not wash their hands before eating. Jesus says they set aside God’s command for their tradition. What comes out of the mouth defiles a person, not what goes in. He travels to the region of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman begs him to heal her daughter. He says he was sent to Israel, and she keeps asking. He praises her faith and heals the girl. Back in Galilee he heals many and feeds four thousand.
events.detail: Jesus says it is not right to give the children’s bread to dogs (verse 26). She does not reject the picture. Verse 27 works inside it. Even the dogs eat what falls from the table. She asks only for crumbs. Verse 28 calls her faith great, and her daughter is healed. A foreign woman’s answer presses past a stated limit.

events.title: Peter recognizes Jesus but rejects the suffering he announces
events.summary: Pharisees and Sadducees ask Jesus for a sign from heaven. He warns his disciples about their teaching. He asks the disciples who they say he is. Peter answers that he is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus blesses him and speaks of building his assembly. Then he says he must suffer, be killed, and rise. Peter rebukes him, and Jesus calls him a stumbling block. Anyone who follows him must take up a cross.
events.detail: Peter gives the right answer in verse 16 and is blessed for it. In verse 22 he tells Jesus that suffering must never happen. Verse 23 uses the harshest words in the chapter for the same man. Peter is thinking in human terms. He knows who Jesus is and rejects the path Jesus names. Knowing the title is not the same as accepting what it means. Verses 24–25 apply that path to every follower.

events.title: The mountain's glory does not remove the coming suffering
events.summary: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. His face shines like the sun, and Moses and Elijah appear with him. Peter offers to build three shelters. A bright cloud covers them, and a voice calls Jesus the beloved Son. The disciples fall down afraid, and Jesus touches them. He tells them to say nothing until he has risen. Below, he heals a boy the disciples could not heal. He again says he will be killed and raised.
events.detail: The voice in verse 5 repeats the words spoken at Jesus’s baptism (3:17). It adds a command: “Listen to him.” What he has just said is that he must suffer (16:21). On the way down he speaks of it again (verses 9 and 12). Verses 22–23 repeat it once more, and the disciples grieve. The glory on the mountain does not cancel that path. It tells them to trust the one who walks it.

events.summary: Pharisees test Jesus with a question about divorce. He points them to the beginning, when God joined man and woman. People bring children, and he blesses them. A rich young man asks what good thing he must do to have eternal life. He says he has kept the commandments. Jesus tells him to sell what he has and give to the poor. The young man goes away sad. Jesus says the last will be first.
events.detail: The young man asks what he still lacks (verse 20). Verse 21 answers with one demand and one invitation. He should sell his goods, give to the poor, and follow. Verse 22 says he left sad, since he owned much. His sadness shows where the cost lay. He had kept the rules and could not let go of his wealth. Verse 26 says such a change is possible only with God.

events.title: Equal pay and serving challenge the pursuit of rank
events.summary: Jesus tells of a landowner who hires workers at dawn for a day’s wage. He hires more at later hours, even an hour before sunset. At evening each receives the same wage. Those hired first complain. Jesus again foretells his death and resurrection. The mother of James and John asks for the best seats for her sons. Jesus says the great must be servants. He gives sight to two blind men near Jericho.
events.detail: The first workers received exactly what they agreed to (verse 13). No one cheated them. Verse 12 states their real complaint. The owner made the latecomers “equal to us.” They resent another’s gain, not their own loss. The owner asks whether his generosity makes them envious (verse 15). The request for the best seats shows the same concern for rank (verses 20–21).

events.title: The vineyard accusation names its immediate hearers
events.summary: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, and crowds shout “Hosanna.” He drives the traders out of the temple and heals there. The chief priests ask by what authority he acts. He answers with a question about John’s baptism. He tells of two sons, only one of whom obeys. He tells of tenants who kill the owner’s servants and then his son. He says the Kingdom will be given to others. The leaders want to arrest him and fear the crowds.
events.detail: The vineyard story uses a picture from Isaiah 5:1–7. In it the tenants refuse to give the owner his fruit. Verse 45 says who understood themselves to be the target. The chief priests and the Pharisees saw that he meant them. The charge is aimed at those leaders in that place. Verse 46 shows the crowds on the other side, holding Jesus to be a prophet. The story should not be read as a charge against a whole people.

events.title: Tests about taxes and resurrection lead to love as the law's center
events.summary: Jesus tells of a king whose invited guests refuse his son’s wedding feast. The Pharisees ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. He says to give Caesar what is Caesar’s and God what is God’s. The Sadducees ask about marriage in the resurrection. He says God is the God of the living. A lawyer asks which commandment is greatest. Jesus names love for God and love for neighbor. He then asks how the Christ can be David’s son and David’s Lord.
events.detail: The lawyer asks for one great commandment (verse 36). Jesus gives two and joins them. The first is from Deuteronomy 6:5, and the second from Leviticus 19:18. Verse 40 says all the law and the prophets “depend” on these. The word pictures something hanging from a peg. Every other command hangs from love of God and neighbor. They are the measure for reading the rest.

events.title: The accusation examines burdens, display, and neglected justice
events.summary: Jesus speaks to the crowds and his disciples about the scribes and Pharisees. They teach the law and do not practice it. They load others with heavy burdens and love titles and honor. He pronounces a series of woes on them. They shut the Kingdom against people. They tithe small herbs and neglect justice, mercy, and faith. They are like whitewashed tombs. He grieves over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets.
events.detail: Verse 23 gives an example of careful obedience. These teachers tithe even garden herbs. Jesus does not tell them to stop. He says they “ought to have done” the weightier things as well. Those are justice, mercy, and faith. Small duties have crowded out large ones. Verse 37 shows that the speech ends in grief over the city.

events.title: Readiness means faithful care during an uncertain wait
events.summary: Jesus says the temple’s stones will all be thrown down. On the Mount of Olives his disciples ask when and what the sign will be. He warns of false christs, wars, famines, and persecution. They must flee when they see the desolating sacrilege. The Son of Man will come like lightning. No one knows the day or hour, not even the angels. As in Noah’s days, people will be caught unaware. So they must watch and be ready.
events.detail: The disciples ask for a date and a sign (verse 3). Verse 36 says the day is unknown. Verses 45–51 then describe what readiness looks like. A servant is set over the household to give them food on time. The faithful one is found doing that when his master returns. The bad servant beats the others and gets drunk. Being ready means caring for people during the wait.

events.title: The waiting stories end with care for people in need
events.summary: Jesus tells of ten young women waiting with lamps for a bridegroom. Five run out of oil and are shut out. He tells of a man who entrusts money to three servants. Two put it to work, and one buries it. Then he describes the Son of Man on his throne. He separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Some fed the hungry, welcomed strangers, and visited prisoners. The King says they did it to him.
events.detail: Both groups in the last scene are surprised. The first asks when they saw the King hungry or in prison (verses 37–39). The second asks the same question (verse 44). Neither knew who was in front of them. Verse 40 gives the King’s explanation. What was done for the least of his brothers was done for him. The chapter’s stories of waiting end with care for people in need.

events.title: Jesus' arrest reveals failed promises and rejected force
events.summary: The chief priests plot to kill Jesus, and a woman anoints him with costly oil. Judas agrees to hand him over for thirty pieces of silver. Jesus eats the Passover with the twelve and gives them bread and the cup. Peter promises never to deny him. In Gethsemane Jesus prays while the disciples sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd, and Jesus is arrested. The council condemns him for blasphemy. Peter denies knowing him three times and weeps.
events.detail: A crowd comes with swords and clubs (verse 47). One of Jesus’s companions draws a sword and strikes (verse 51). Verse 52 tells him to put it away. Those who take the sword will die by it. Jesus says he could call on legions of angels (verse 53). He refuses force from his own side as well. Verse 56 then says all the disciples left him and fled.

events.title: The governor's handwashing does not stop his order
events.summary: Jesus is handed to Pilate, the governor. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself. Pilate questions Jesus and offers to release a prisoner. The crowd asks for Barabbas. Pilate washes his hands and says he is innocent of this blood. Soldiers mock Jesus with a robe, a crown of thorns, and a reed. He is crucified between two robbers and dies. Joseph of Arimathea buries him, and the tomb is sealed and guarded.
events.detail: Pilate’s wife warns him that Jesus is righteous (verse 19). Pilate himself sees that envy lies behind the charge (verse 18). In verse 24 he washes his hands in front of the crowd. Verse 26 then reports what he does. He has Jesus flogged and hands him over to be crucified. The order is his. A public gesture does not undo the act that follows it.

events.title: The final promise sends uncertain disciples beyond the earlier boundary
events.summary: At dawn after the Sabbath two women come to the tomb. An angel rolls back the stone and tells them Jesus has risen. They run to tell the disciples and meet Jesus on the way. The guards are paid to say the body was stolen. The eleven go to a mountain in Galilee. They worship him, though some doubt. He says all authority has been given to him. He sends them to make disciples of all nations and promises to be with them.
events.detail: Verse 17 says the eleven worshiped and that some doubted. Jesus sends them anyway. In 10:5–6 he sent them only to Israel. Verse 19 now sends them to all nations. Verse 20 closes the book with a promise: “I am with you always.” The book opened with the name Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23). The promise that began it also ends it.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study. Luke 10:30 sets a parable on the way down from Jerusalem to Jericho.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.

regions.name: Herod’s kingdom · approximate
regions.summary: Herod the Great ruled as king under Rome from 37 to 4 BCE. His kingdom held Judea, Samaria, Galilee, and lands east of the Jordan.
regions.detail: Matthew 2 sets Jesus’ birth in Herod’s days. After Herod dies, his son Archelaus rules Judea (Matthew 2:22).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the regions the article lists.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Pontius Pilate governs Judea in the Gospels (Luke 3:1). He tries Jesus in Jerusalem.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Galilee · under Herod Antipas
regions.summary: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea until 39 CE.
regions.detail: Jesus grows up and teaches in Galilee under Antipas. Antipas kills John the Baptist (Mark 6).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to Galilee.

regions.name: Perea · under Herod Antipas
regions.summary: Perea lay east of the Jordan, across from Judea and Samaria. Herod Antipas ruled it with Galilee.
regions.detail: Matthew 19:1 and Mark 10:1 take Jesus beyond the Jordan. He is on his way to Jerusalem.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The Gospels do not use the name Perea.

regions.name: Philip’s lands · approximate
regions.summary: Philip, another son of Herod, ruled lands northeast of the Jordan until 34 CE.
regions.detail: Luke 3:1 names Philip as tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis. A tetrarch ruled one part of a divided kingdom.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Syria took these lands after Philip died.

regions.name: Decapolis · approximate
regions.summary: The Decapolis was a group of ten Greek-style cities, most east of the Jordan. Each ran itself under Rome.
regions.detail: Crowds from the Decapolis follow Jesus (Matthew 4:25). The healed man of Mark 5 tells his story there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape covers the southern cities only. Some scholars doubt the cities formed one league.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Luke 2:2 dates a census by Quirinius, governor of Syria. Jesus visits the coast near Tyre and Sidon in Mark 7:24.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

guides.title: Matthew: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Repaired relationships belong before the offering
steps.text: Verses 21–22 trace murder back to anger and insult. Verses 23–24 then give a case. A person stands at the altar with an offering. He remembers that a brother has something against him. The verse does not ask who was at fault. He must leave the gift and go to be reconciled first. Worship waits for the repaired relationship.

steps.title: Care for the small and mercy for debtors answer the rank question
steps.text: The first servant owed ten thousand talents, a sum no one could repay (verse 24). The second owed a hundred denarii, a few months’ wages (verse 28). The king forgave the larger debt entirely. Verse 33 asks the question the story turns on. Should the forgiven man not have shown the same mercy? Forgiveness received was meant to change how he treated others. The chapter began with a question about rank and ends here.

steps.title: The governor's handwashing does not stop his order
steps.text: Pilate’s wife warns him that Jesus is righteous (verse 19). Pilate himself sees that envy lies behind the charge (verse 18). In verse 24 he washes his hands in front of the crowd. Verse 26 then reports what he does. He has Jesus flogged and hands him over to be crucified. The order is his. A public gesture does not undo the act that follows it.

steps.title: The final promise sends uncertain disciples beyond the earlier boundary
steps.text: Verse 17 says the eleven worshiped and that some doubted. Jesus sends them anyway. In 10:5–6 he sent them only to Israel. Verse 19 now sends them to all nations. Verse 20 closes the book with a promise: “I am with you always.” The book opened with the name Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23). The promise that began it also ends it.

chapterMaps.narrative: Matthew opens with the family line of Jesus Christ, son of David and Abraham. It runs in three sets of fourteen generations. Four women appear in it: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Uriah’s wife. Mary is pledged to Joseph and is found with child by the Holy Spirit. Joseph plans to end the engagement quietly. An angel tells him in a dream to take Mary as his wife. The child will be named Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins. Joseph does as he is told.

chapterMaps.narrative: Wise men from the east come to Jerusalem seeking the newborn king of the Jews. King Herod is troubled and learns the Christ should be born in Bethlehem. The star leads the wise men to the child, and they worship him with gifts. A dream warns them not to return to Herod. An angel tells Joseph to flee to Egypt with the child and his mother. Herod kills the young boys of Bethlehem. After Herod dies, Joseph brings the family back. They settle in Nazareth in Galilee.

chapterMaps.narrative: John the Baptist preaches in the desert of Judea. He tells people to repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is near. He wears camel’s hair and eats locusts and wild honey. Crowds come and are baptized in the Jordan, confessing their sins. He warns the Pharisees and Sadducees to bear fruit that fits repentance. They must not rely on having Abraham as their father. Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized. The Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice calls him God’s beloved Son.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Spirit leads Jesus into the desert, where he fasts forty days. The devil tells him to turn stones into bread. He tells him to throw himself from the temple and trust the angels. He offers all the world’s kingdoms in return for worship. Jesus answers each time from Deuteronomy. He then begins to preach in Galilee. He calls four fishermen, who leave their nets and follow him. He heals the sick, and great crowds gather.

He has come to fulfill the law, not to destroy it. Anger and insult are judged along with murder. He speaks about lust, divorce, oaths, and revenge. He tells them to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. They are to be complete, as their Father is.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, and crowds shout “Hosanna.” He drives the traders out of the temple and heals there. The chief priests ask by what authority he acts. He answers with a question about John’s baptism. He tells of two sons, only one of whom obeys. He tells of tenants who kill the owner’s servants and then his son. He says the Kingdom will be given to others. The leaders want to arrest him and fear the crowds.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jesus tells of a king whose invited guests refuse his son’s wedding feast. The Pharisees ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. He says to give Caesar what is Caesar’s and God what is God’s. The Sadducees ask about marriage in the resurrection. He says God is the God of the living. A lawyer asks which commandment is greatest. Jesus names love for God and love for neighbor. He then asks how the Christ can be David’s son and David’s Lord.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jesus speaks to the crowds and his disciples about the scribes and Pharisees. They teach the law and do not practice it. They load others with heavy burdens and love titles and honor. He pronounces a series of woes on them. They shut the Kingdom against people. They tithe small herbs and neglect justice, mercy, and faith. They are like whitewashed tombs. He grieves over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jesus says the temple’s stones will all be thrown down. On the Mount of Olives his disciples ask when and what the sign will be. He warns of false christs, wars, famines, and persecution. They must flee when they see the desolating sacrilege. The Son of Man will come like lightning. No one knows the day or hour, not even the angels. As in Noah’s days, people will be caught unaware. So they must watch and be ready.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jesus tells of ten young women waiting with lamps for a bridegroom. Five run out of oil and are shut out. He tells of a man who entrusts money to three servants. Two put it to work, and one buries it. Then he describes the Son of Man on his throne. He separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Some fed the hungry, welcomed strangers, and visited prisoners. The King says they did it to him.

chapterMaps.narrative: The chief priests plot to kill Jesus, and a woman anoints him with costly oil. Judas agrees to hand him over for thirty pieces of silver. Jesus eats the Passover with the twelve and gives them bread and the cup. Peter promises never to deny him. In Gethsemane Jesus prays while the disciples sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd, and Jesus is arrested. The council condemns him for blasphemy. Peter denies knowing him three times and weeps.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jesus is handed to Pilate, the governor. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself. Pilate questions Jesus and offers to release a prisoner. The crowd asks for Barabbas. Pilate washes his hands and says he is innocent of this blood. Soldiers mock Jesus with a robe, a crown of thorns, and a reed. He is crucified between two robbers and dies. Joseph of Arimathea buries him, and the tomb is sealed and guarded.

chapterMaps.narrative: At dawn after the Sabbath two women come to the tomb. An angel rolls back the stone and tells them Jesus has risen. They run to tell the disciples and meet Jesus on the way. The guards are paid to say the body was stolen. The eleven go to a mountain in Galilee. They worship him, though some doubt. He says all authority has been given to him. He sends them to make disciples of all nations and promises to be with them.
